name: Jeti-Oguz Gorge
near: Jeti-Oguz village (at the mouth of the gorge, ~16 km from Karakol); the Jeti-Oguz resort settlement is another 12 km up the gorge.
elev: The “Seven Bulls” rock massif ~2140 m; sanatorium 2000–2200 m; upper Kok-Jaiyk valley ~2300–2500 m (central-asia.guide: 2050 m — contradicts other data); “Maiden's Braids/Tears” waterfall ~2500 m; mouth of the gorge at the lake 1603 m.
short: Jeti-Oguz is a gorge with the red “Seven Bulls” and “Broken Heart” rocks, an old radon spa and the alpine Kok-Jaiyk valley, 25–30 km from Karakol.
desc: Jeti-Oguz (“seven bulls”) is a gorge about 30 km long in Terskey Ala-Too, southwest of Karakol. The main sight is a row of bright red sandstone cliffs, the “Seven Bulls”, and a separate rock, the “Broken Heart”, at the entrance to the narrows; according to legend, they are petrified bulls sacrificed by a khan at a feast where a kidnapped beauty died. Above the rocks is the Soviet-era Jeti-Oguz sanatorium (founded 1932, radon baths), and beyond it the Kok-Jaiyk valley with yurts and a trail to the 20 m “Maiden's Braids” waterfall. Tian Shan spruce grows on the slopes. The gorge is a popular day trip from Karakol and the starting point of treks to Ala-Kul over Teleti Pass.
guide: The first thing you meet is the “Broken Heart” — a red rock with a crack at the entrance to the narrows; stop, but the main view is further on: climb the hill opposite the sanatorium, from where the whole row of the “Seven Bulls” is visible against the spruces — in the morning the sun hits the rocks and the red is at its deepest. Further on the road leads to Kok-Jaiyk, an alpine meadow with yurts where shepherds offer horses; poppies bloom here in May. From the meadow it is 1–1.5 km on foot (20–25 min) to the “Maiden's Braids” waterfall along a forest path with handrails. Since summer 2026 locals have restricted car access to Kok-Jaiyk — count on an extra 3 km on foot from the sanatorium or a paid local shuttle. In the sanatorium you can take a radon bath for 100–200 som — a rare chance in the mountains.
see: The “Seven Bulls” and “Broken Heart” rocks; the viewpoint hill opposite the sanatorium (20–30 min climb); the Jeti-Oguz sanatorium with radon baths; the Kok-Jaiyk valley (Valley of Flowers) with yurts; the “Maiden's Braids” waterfall (~20 m); Tian Shan spruces; a view of Boris Yeltsin Peak (5168 m) from the upper reaches.
skip: You only want the “photo rocks” and are short on time — then a 30-minute stop at the Seven Bulls on the way is enough, without the climb to Kok-Jaiyk. You are going in the rainy season (spring/autumn) — the trail to the waterfall gets washed out. You have already seen Skazka Canyon and don't like the yurt “tourist circus” in season.
diff: Easy for a roadside stop at the rocks and the walk to the waterfall (1.5 km, 20–30 min on a trail with a little climbing); moderate for the climb to the viewpoint hill and for treks from Kok-Jaiyk (Teleti Pass ~3800 m is hard).
when: June–September: yurts are open and the trail to the waterfall is dry; May — poppies bloom at Kok-Jaiyk, but the waterfall may be frozen; September — fewer people and golden autumn. The sanatorium is open year-round; in winter there is the Ecotrek winter yurt camp and ski outings, and the waterfall is not accessible.
hours: The gorge and the rocks are open territory, 24 hours. The sanatorium is open year-round. The yurts, cafes and souvenir stalls at Kok-Jaiyk are summer only. The last marshrutka (minibus) to Karakol leaves around 17:00.
daytime: Morning: the sun lights the red rocks from the east, and by lunchtime the contrast fades; at Kok-Jaiyk there are many groups during the day — leave Karakol by 8–9 am. Sunset is beautiful on the way back, with a view of the lake.
how: From Karakol, 16 km west along the highway to Jeti-Oguz village, then turn south and go 12 km up the gorge to the resort (25–30 km in total, 40–60 min). The “Broken Heart” and “Seven Bulls” rocks are by the road before the sanatorium; further on, a dirt road leads to Kok-Jaiyk (3–5 km), then on foot to the waterfall. Public transport: marshrutkas No. 371/366 from Karakol (the Aldasheva/Torgoeva crossroads by the Ak-Tilek bazaar) to the resort. From Bishkek ~400 km.
needcar: Yes as far as the resort (marshrutka/taxi/car); in the gorge, on foot or by horse. Since summer 2026 private cars are restricted from driving to Kok-Jaiyk — the last 3 km are on foot or by the local paid shuttle.
self: Yes: a marshrutka or taxi to the resort, then everything on foot along obvious trails; no permits are needed, and sources from 2022–2026 mention no entrance fee for the gorge. For a night in a yurt it is better to book ahead in season.
roadtype: Paved from Karakol to the sanatorium (including 12 km in the gorge); above the sanatorium a dirt road leads to Kok-Jaiyk — passable by a regular car in dry weather (2025), but from 2026 cars are restricted from entering the jailoo (summer pasture); to the waterfall there is a forest path with handrails, which gets washed out in the rains. TripAdvisor: “the road to the Seven Bulls is not very good”.
traveltime: Karakol → resort 40–60 min (25–30 km); resort → Kok-Jaiyk 10–15 min by car or ~1 h on foot; meadow → waterfall 20–25 min on foot; viewpoint hill — up to 30 min; the “Broken Heart” — a 20 min walk. Allow half a day to a day for the whole gorge.
stay: Jeti-Oguz sanatorium (radon spa, year-round; ~740 som/person in a double in 2017, ~1500 ₽/night in 2022); yurt camps at Kok-Jaiyk — booking via nomads-yurt.com (price did not load), Ecotrek Yurt Camp (Destination Karakol, also in winter); guesthouses in Jeti-Oguz village — Emir's Guesthouse ~1230 som/room, Kok Jaiyk Guesthouse 650–800 som, yurt 400 som/person (2017). Current 2025–2026 prices are not published — check.
net: Almost everywhere in the gorge up to the sanatorium and at Kok-Jaiyk there is good mobile signal and 4G (dorogi-ne-dorogi.ru, updated 06.2025); higher up, at the waterfall and on the passes, the signal disappears.
entry: No source from 2022–2026 mentions an entrance fee for the gorge (2022 travel stories: “we paid nothing to enter”). A radon bath in the sanatorium is 100 som/15 min (2017) / 200 som (2023). A fee for driving to Kok-Jaiyk (barrier) is possible from 2026 — the amount has not been published.
transfer: Marshrutka ~100 som (2017, current price not confirmed); shared taxi 150–350 som/person (2017); guided excursion from Karakol/Cholpon-Ata ~€240–243 per group of up to 4 (2025–2026).
bring: Footwear for the waterfall trail (wet, roots), a rain jacket, a windproof layer (2200–2500 m), cash for yurts, cafes and baths, a swimsuit and towel for the radon baths, water and a snack (food at Kok-Jaiyk is only available in summer).
warn:
Since 21.07.2025 there has been an eco-checkpoint at the entrance to Kok-Jaiyk: private cars are not allowed onto the pasture (24.kg). Go up on foot, on horseback or by permitted transport.

Since summer 2026 locals have restricted car access to Kok-Jaiyk — the last 3 km from the sanatorium are on foot or by paid shuttle; check on the spot. The trail to the waterfall is slippery after rain and gets washed out in spring/autumn. In season there are many groups and horses; dogs near the yurts. The information on guesthouses is inconsistent: Too.kg wrote that there is no accommodation in the gorge, while local organizations publish options — book ahead.
food: At Kok-Jaiyk in summer, in the yurts: kumys, boorsoks, lagman, shashlik; in the sanatorium — a canteen; in Jeti-Oguz village — shops and simple cafes (lunch ~130 som in 2017). Bring ashlyan-fu, the Dungan cold noodle dish, from Karakol.
reviews: 2GIS: 4.9/5, 317 ratings, 75 reviews (viewed 07.10.2026). TripAdvisor “Jeti-Oguz Canyon (Seven Bulls Rocks)”: 4.5/5, 146 reviews, No. 3 of 96 attractions in the region (07.10.2026). Pluses: red rocks against spruces and the river, a beautiful valley, yurts; minuses: a bad road near the rocks, part of the infrastructure is abandoned, and it takes time to reach the waterfall.
p.sum: The easiest day trip from Karakol (25–30 km, 40–60 min): paved road to the sanatorium, with the “Broken Heart” and “Seven Bulls” rocks right by the road. Without a car — marshrutka No. 371/355 from the southwest corner of the Karakol bazaar (the Torgoeva/Aldasheva crossing, departing ≈10:00 and around noon) or a taxi via a guesthouse (≈700 som, waiting 100 som/h). Above the sanatorium it is 6–8 km of dirt road and five small bridges to the Kok-Jaiyk yurts (since 07.2025 there is an eco-checkpoint at the entrance and private cars are not allowed onto the jailoo — you leave the car in the parking area and walk to the yurts), and from there 2.5 km to the waterfall. It is worth spending the night in a yurt at Kok-Jaiyk (from $13) or in the sanatorium itself (≈$10/night, radon baths).

p.iti.1.title: 2 days with an overnight stay
p.iti.1.plan: Day 1: the rocks, the sanatorium, the climb to Kok-Jaiyk, a night in a yurt (Kok Zhaiyk/Ecotrek). Day 2: the waterfall in the morning, a horse ride across the meadows, and on the way back — Chon-Kyzyl-Suu or Barskoon along the south shore.
p.iti.2.title: Combinations
p.iti.2.plan: Karakol → Jeti-Oguz → Kyzyl-Suu (Chon-Kyzyl-Suu) → Juuku → Barskoon → Skazka — one day along the south shore by car with a driver (≈5000 som, 2024); on foot — Jeti-Oguz ↔ Karakol gorge over Teleti, ↔ Chon-Kyzyl-Suu over Archa-Tor.
p.season: May: poppies at Kok-Jaiyk, the waterfall may be frozen, the yurts open. June–August: peak, the yurts are working, many groups — arrive by 8–9 am. September — early October: golden autumn, fewer people. November–April: the sanatorium is open, Ecotrek winter yurt camp, freeride and snowshoeing; the waterfall trail is closed.
p.budget.economy: ≈2000–3000 som/person: round-trip marshrutka ≈100–200, yurt ≈700–1300 ($13 per yurt for three), food 600–1000, radon bath 100–200.
p.budget.comfort: ≈8000–15,000 som/person: taxi/MYWAY (8000 per car) or a €240 tour per group, Ecotrek $50 with breakfast + dinner $15, a horse ride (from 800 som to £117).
p.permits: Not needed. Entry to the gorge is free. Since 21.07.2025 there has been an eco-checkpoint at Kok-Jaiyk: cars are not let onto the jailoo, and you go to the yurts on foot from the parking area (the fee amount is not published).
p.access: The rocks and the sanatorium are accessible to everyone, including older people and children (view from the road). With a wheelchair — only at the sanatorium. The waterfall trail — children from 5–6 years old, slippery after rain. With a dog — allowed, but there are shepherd dogs near the yurts.
